intro: Chronic paediatric conditions covers the long-term illnesses GPs and paediatricians manage every day: asthma, food allergy, type 1 diabetes and obesity, epilepsy, cystic fibrosis, ADHD, and acute rheumatic fever with rheumatic heart disease. The AMC tests diagnosis, first-line Australian management, school and family support, and the parts that differ from India, such as ASCIA action plans, CF newborn screening, state stimulant regulation and ARF in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.

lessons.title: Childhood asthma
objectives: Diagnose asthma in children and distinguish it from preschool viral wheeze and other causes of wheeze
Decide when a child needs a preventer and choose it by age using the Australian Asthma Handbook
Teach inhaler and spacer technique and write an asthma action plan
Assess asthma control and troubleshoot poor control before stepping up

sections.heading: Why asthma is a core AMC topic
sections.body:
Asthma is the most common chronic disease of Australian children, affecting roughly **1 in 10**. Australia's rates are among the highest in the world, and asthma is a leading cause of paediatric hospital admission and school absence. Deaths still occur, usually in children with poor control, poor adherence or delayed treatment. Most care happens in **general practice**, guided by the **National Asthma Council's Australian Asthma Handbook** (AAH).

In Australia every child with asthma should have a **written asthma action plan**, and schools and childcare services keep asthma plans and emergency reliever kits. Acute severe asthma is covered in paediatric emergencies; this lesson is about diagnosis and long-term control.

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.body:
Asthma is **chronic airway inflammation** (usually eosinophilic, Th2-driven in atopic children) causing **variable airflow obstruction** through bronchial smooth muscle contraction, mucosal oedema and mucus plugging, with **airway hyperresponsiveness** to triggers.

- **Triggers**: viral URTIs (the commonest trigger in young children), exercise, cold air, allergens (house dust mite, pollens, pets, moulds), tobacco smoke and vaping, bushfire smoke, and **thunderstorm asthma** (a Victorian phenomenon: ryegrass pollen ruptured by storms; the 2016 Melbourne epidemic).
- **Atopy**: asthma clusters with eczema, allergic rhinitis and food allergy (the "atopic march").
- Because the problem is inflammation, **inhaled corticosteroids** (ICS) are the backbone of prevention; relievers treat the bronchospasm but not the underlying disease.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
sections.body:
**Typical features**: recurrent wheeze, cough (especially **at night and with exercise**), breathlessness and chest tightness; symptoms vary over time and are triggered; personal or family history of atopy; response to bronchodilator.

**Preschool children (1-5 years)**: many wheeze only with viral infections (**episodic viral wheeze**) and outgrow it. Asthma cannot be confirmed with spirometry at this age, so the AAH describes patterns rather than a firm diagnosis: wheeze only with colds vs wheeze between colds (multiple-trigger wheeze), and atopy increases the chance of persistent asthma.

**Children 6 and over**: confirm with **spirometry** where possible, showing **reversible airflow limitation** (FEV1 increase of at least 12% after bronchodilator). Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma.

**Differentials** (think of them when features are atypical):

| Clue | Consider |
|---|---|
| Sudden onset after choking, unilateral wheeze | **Inhaled foreign body** |
| Wet cough for over 4 weeks, no wheeze | **Protracted bacterial bronchitis**, bronchiectasis |
| Failure to thrive, steatorrhoea, recurrent chest infections | **Cystic fibrosis** |
| Wheeze from birth, stridor, feeding issues | Structural airway abnormality, vascular ring |
| Infant under 12 months with first wheeze and coryza | **Bronchiolitis** |
| Inspiratory noise, throat tightness with exercise in an adolescent athlete | **Inducible laryngeal obstruction** (vocal cord dysfunction) |
| Cough only, no other features | Post-viral cough, upper airway cough |

sections.heading: Long-term management
sections.body:
**Relievers**: short-acting beta-2 agonist (**salbutamol**) via **pMDI and spacer** for all ages (with a face mask for children too young to use a mouthpiece, usually under about 4). Spacers deliver as well as nebulisers.

**When to start a preventer** (AAH principle): not every child with asthma needs one. Consider a preventer when symptoms are **frequent** (for example, recurring several times a week or waking at night), when the child has had **flare-ups needing oral corticosteroids or ED visits**, or when asthma limits activity. Follow the AAH for exact thresholds by age.

| Age | First-line preventer | If still uncontrolled |
|---|---|---|
| 1-5 years | **Montelukast** or **low-dose ICS** (trial, then review) | Specialist referral |
| 6-11 years | **Low-dose ICS** (montelukast an alternative) | Check adherence and technique, then increase ICS, add montelukast or use ICS/LABA; consider referral |
| 12 years and over | Low-dose ICS, or **as-needed low-dose budesonide-formoterol** (anti-inflammatory reliever) for mild asthma | Maintenance-and-reliever ICS-formoterol, higher doses, specialist |

**Monitoring and side effects**: low-dose ICS may slightly reduce growth velocity (about 0.5-1 cm, mostly in the first year) but the benefit outweighs this; use the lowest effective dose and rinse the mouth after use. Montelukast can cause **neuropsychiatric effects** (sleep disturbance, agitation, mood changes), so parents should be warned.

**Assessing control** at every visit: daytime symptoms, reliever use, night waking, activity limitation, and flare-ups. **Before stepping up, check**:
1. **Inhaler technique** (most common problem)
2. **Adherence** (collected scripts, honest conversation)
3. **Triggers and exposure** (smoking or vaping at home, allergens)
4. **Comorbidities** (allergic rhinitis, obesity, reflux)
5. **Is it really asthma?**

**Written asthma action plan**: what to take every day, how to recognise worsening, what to do in a flare-up (increase reliever, when to start oral prednisolone if prescribed, when to seek help), and emergency steps. **Asthma first aid** (National Asthma Council): sit upright, **4 separate puffs of reliever via spacer (1 puff, 4 breaths, repeat)**, wait 4 minutes, repeat 4 puffs; if no improvement call **000** and keep giving 4 puffs every 4 minutes.

Also: annual influenza vaccination, smoke-free home, review after every ED visit, and a school action plan.

**Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction**: cough or wheeze during or just after exercise. Taking salbutamol 5-20 minutes before exercise helps, and a proper warm-up reduces symptoms. If a child needs a reliever for exercise most days, that is a sign asthma is **not well controlled** and the preventer should be reviewed, not a reason to stop sport. Encourage children with asthma to be fully active.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Frequent night cough and reliever use several times a week in a 7-year-old: **start low-dose ICS** and an action plan.
- Poor control on ICS: the right next step is usually **check technique and adherence**, not "double the dose".
- Spacer over nebuliser for home and most acute care.
- Wet cough without wheeze for weeks is not asthma.
- Asthma first aid: **4 puffs, 4 breaths each, wait 4 minutes**.
- Montelukast: warn about neuropsychiatric side effects.

keyPoints: Asthma affects about 1 in 10 Australian children; most care is in general practice.
Spirometry from about age 6: FEV1 rise of at least 12% after bronchodilator supports asthma.
Preschool wheeze is often episodic viral wheeze; atopy predicts persistence.
Preventer when symptoms are frequent or flare-ups need oral steroids; low-dose ICS first-line from age 6.
Always use a pMDI with spacer; face mask in young children.
Check technique, adherence and triggers before stepping up.
Every child needs a written asthma action plan; asthma first aid is 4 puffs, wait 4 minutes.
redFlags: Night waking and reliever use most days despite preventer
Flare-up needing oral steroids or ED visit
Unilateral wheeze or wheeze after choking
Failure to thrive or chronic wet cough

contrast.india: Nebulisers and syrups (oral salbutamol) still common.
contrast.australia: pMDI with spacer for all ages; oral salbutamol not recommended.
Written asthma action plan for every child, with copies for school and childcare.

flashcards.back: FEV1 increase of at least 12% after bronchodilator.

flashcards.front: First-line preventer for a 7-year-old with frequent asthma symptoms?
flashcards.back: Low-dose inhaled corticosteroid.

flashcards.front: Asthma first aid (National Asthma Council)?
flashcards.back: Sit upright; 4 puffs via spacer (1 puff, 4 breaths each), wait 4 minutes, repeat; call 000 if no improvement.

flashcards.front: Most common reason for poor asthma control on a preventer?
flashcards.back: Poor inhaler technique or poor adherence.

flashcards.back: Neuropsychiatric effects: sleep disturbance, agitation, mood change.

quiz.stem: An 8-year-old boy has had a dry cough at night and wheeze with sport for several months. He uses salbutamol 4-5 days a week and wakes at night with cough about twice a week. He has eczema. Spirometry shows a 15% rise in FEV1 after bronchodilator. He has never had a preventer. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Continue salbutamol as needed only
Start oral prednisolone for 5 days
Start a long-acting beta-agonist alone
Start regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid via spacer and provide a written asthma action plan
Start nebulised salbutamol twice daily
quiz.explanation:
He has confirmed asthma (typical symptoms, atopy and **reversibility of 15%**) with **frequent symptoms** and **night waking**, so reliever-only treatment is not enough. The Australian Asthma Handbook recommends a **regular low-dose inhaled corticosteroid** as first-line preventer for children aged 6-11, delivered by **pMDI with spacer**, plus a **written asthma action plan**.

Review in 4-6 weeks to check control, technique and adherence. A LABA must never be used without an ICS because LABA monotherapy is associated with severe asthma events.
whyWrong: Frequent symptoms and night waking mean he needs a preventer.
Oral steroids treat flare-ups, not ongoing control.
LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma.
Nebulisers are not needed for maintenance and salbutamol is not a preventer.

quiz.stem: A 10-year-old girl has been on low-dose inhaled fluticasone for 6 months but still uses her reliever most days and has had two ED visits. Her mother says she takes the preventer 'most mornings'. When asked to demonstrate, she takes the puffer without a spacer, inhales before pressing the canister, and does not hold her breath. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Correct her inhaler technique with a spacer and address adherence, then review
Double the dose of inhaled corticosteroid
Add oral montelukast
Refer for a sweat test
Switch to a nebulised preventer
quiz.explanation:
Before stepping up asthma treatment, always check **inhaler technique, adherence, triggers and the diagnosis**. This girl has clearly poor technique (no spacer, poor coordination, no breath hold), so very little drug reaches her lungs, and her adherence is uncertain.

The next step is to **teach technique with a spacer**, address adherence (a routine, reminders, understanding why a preventer is needed daily), check exposure to smoke and allergens, update her action plan, and review in 4-6 weeks. Only if still uncontrolled would treatment be stepped up.
whyWrong: Increasing the dose won't help if little drug reaches the lungs.
Adding a drug before fixing technique and adherence is premature.
Nothing here suggests CF; she has typical asthma with poor technique.
A spacer is as effective as a nebuliser for most children.

quiz.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had four episodes of wheeze and cough over the past year, each starting with a cold and settling within a week with salbutamol via spacer and mask. Between episodes he is completely well, running around without cough or wheeze, and sleeps well. He has no eczema or food allergy. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Start regular inhaled corticosteroid
Arrange spirometry
Prescribe oral salbutamol syrup for future episodes
Refer to a respiratory paediatrician
Continue salbutamol via spacer and mask as needed for episodes, with a written action plan and review
quiz.explanation:
This pattern is **episodic viral wheeze**: wheeze only with colds and completely well between episodes, with no atopy. It is common in preschoolers and most children outgrow it as their airways grow.

Management is **salbutamol via pMDI, spacer and mask** as needed during episodes, a written plan, avoiding smoke exposure, and review. **Regular preventers are not routinely needed** for infrequent episodic viral wheeze; the AAH suggests considering a trial if episodes are frequent or severe.

Spirometry is not reliable under about age 6, and oral salbutamol is not recommended (slower, more side effects).
whyWrong: Regular ICS is not routinely indicated for infrequent episodic viral wheeze.
Spirometry is unreliable at this age.
Oral salbutamol is less effective with more side effects.
Referral is not needed for a typical, mild pattern.

lessons.title: Food allergy in children
objectives: Distinguish IgE-mediated from non-IgE-mediated food allergy by timing and features
Interpret skin prick tests and specific IgE sensibly, knowing that sensitisation is not allergy
Give ASCIA advice on introducing allergenic foods to infants
Manage a child at risk of anaphylaxis with an ASCIA action plan, autoinjector and school planning

sections.heading: Australia's allergy problem
sections.body:
Australia has some of the highest rates of childhood food allergy in the world. In Melbourne's **HealthNuts** study, **over 10% of 1-year-olds** had challenge-proven food allergy (egg and peanut most commonly). Risk factors include **infant eczema** (especially early-onset and severe), family history of allergy, and delayed introduction of allergenic foods. East Asian heritage and living in southern Australia (lower vitamin D) have also been associated.

The national body is **ASCIA** (Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy). Its action plans, infant feeding guidance and school guidelines are what the AMC expects you to know.

sections.heading: Types of food allergy
sections.body:
| Type | Mechanism | Timing | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IgE-mediated** | Specific IgE on mast cells | **Minutes to 2 hours** | Hives, lip swelling, vomiting, wheeze, **anaphylaxis**; peanut, tree nut, egg, milk, sesame, fish, shellfish, wheat, soy |
| **Non-IgE-mediated** | Cell-mediated | Hours to days | **FPIES** (profuse vomiting 1-4 hours after trigger, pallor, lethargy), food protein-induced proctocolitis (blood-streaked stools in a well breastfed infant), enteropathy |
| **Mixed** | Both | Variable | **Eosinophilic oesophagitis** (dysphagia, food bolus impaction in older children), atopic eczema flares |

**Food intolerance** (for example lactose intolerance after gastroenteritis) is not allergy: it is not immune-mediated and cannot cause anaphylaxis.

**Why early introduction works**: the "dual allergen exposure" hypothesis. Exposure through **inflamed, eczematous skin** tends to cause sensitisation; exposure through the **gut** tends to cause tolerance. The LEAP trial showed that early peanut introduction in high-risk infants markedly reduced peanut allergy. That reversed older advice to delay allergenic foods.

sections.heading: Testing: history first
sections.body:
- **The history is the most important test**: which food, how much, how quickly symptoms began, what the symptoms were, and whether the food has been tolerated since.
- **Skin prick test (SPT)** or **serum specific IgE** confirm **sensitisation**. A positive test **does not mean allergy**: many sensitised children tolerate the food. Larger wheals or higher IgE levels increase the likelihood of true allergy.
- **Do not order broad "food panels"** without a history; they produce false positives that lead to unnecessary food avoidance and nutritional problems.
- **Oral food challenge** under specialist supervision is the **gold standard** and is used to confirm allergy or tolerance (especially to see whether a child has outgrown an allergy).
- Unproven tests (IgG food testing, kinesiology, hair analysis, Vega testing) have no role; ASCIA specifically warns against them.
- FPIES is a clinical diagnosis; SPT and IgE are usually negative.

sections.heading: Managing the food-allergic child
sections.body:
**Avoidance and education**: label reading (Australian food labelling must declare common allergens), eating out, "may contain" statements, and cross-contamination. A dietitian helps avoid nutritional deficiency, especially in milk allergy.

**ASCIA action plans**:
- **Red ASCIA Action Plan for Anaphylaxis**: for children prescribed an **adrenaline autoinjector** (those with previous anaphylaxis, or considered at high risk, such as peanut/tree nut allergy with asthma).
- **Green ASCIA Action Plan for Allergic Reactions**: for children with allergy not prescribed an autoinjector.
- Autoinjector dose: **150 microg for 7.5-20 kg, 300 microg for over 20 kg**. Autoinjectors are PBS-subsidised; families are trained and plans are shared with school and childcare.

**Schools and childcare**: individual health care plans, staff training in anaphylaxis, and general-use autoinjectors. Blanket "nut bans" are not recommended by ASCIA because they create false security; risk minimisation strategies are preferred.

**Cow's milk protein allergy in infants**:
- Breastfeeding: continue; mother may need to exclude dairy in some cases (non-IgE forms), with dietitian support and calcium.
- Formula-fed: **extensively hydrolysed formula** first-line; **amino acid formula** for severe or anaphylactic cases, or if hydrolysed fails.
- **Soy formula** is not recommended under 6 months; **goat's milk and other mammalian milks** are unsuitable (cross-reactive).
- Most children **outgrow milk and egg allergy** (often by school age), usually confirmed by supervised reintroduction or challenge. A ladder approach to baked milk or egg may be used under specialist guidance.
- **Peanut, tree nut, sesame, fish and shellfish** allergy usually persists (only about 20% outgrow peanut allergy).

**Oral immunotherapy**: offered in some specialist centres and trials for peanut allergy, not in general practice.

**Asthma control** is crucial because asthma is the main risk factor for fatal anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: Infant feeding advice (ASCIA)
sections.body:
ASCIA's advice for **all infants**, including those at high risk of allergy:
- **Introduce solid foods around 6 months, but not before 4 months**, when the infant shows signs of readiness.
- **Introduce common allergenic foods, including smooth peanut butter/paste and well-cooked egg, in the first year of life** (by 12 months). Do not delay.
- Once introduced, **keep giving them regularly** (about twice a week) to maintain tolerance.
- Hydrolysed (partially hydrolysed) formula is no longer recommended for allergy prevention.
- Continue breastfeeding while solids are introduced.
- Manage eczema actively (emollients, topical corticosteroids), since skin inflammation drives sensitisation.
- **Screening tests before introducing foods are not recommended** for most infants; infants with severe eczema or known egg allergy may benefit from medical advice first, but should not have introduction delayed unnecessarily.
- Whole nuts are a choking hazard under 5 years; use smooth pastes.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Parent asks when to introduce peanut: **in the first year, around 6 months (not before 4 months), and keep it in the diet**.
- Positive SPT to a food the child eats without symptoms: **not allergic**; keep eating it.
- Repetitive vomiting and pallor 2 hours after rice cereal, no rash: **FPIES**, not anaphylaxis; no adrenaline, IV fluids if severe.
- Blood-streaked stools in a thriving breastfed infant: **food protein-induced proctocolitis** (cow's milk usually).
- Milk-allergic infant on formula: **extensively hydrolysed formula**, not soy (under 6 months) or goat milk.
- Autoinjector doses and the red vs green ASCIA plans.

keyPoints: Over 10% of Melbourne 1-year-olds had challenge-proven food allergy (HealthNuts).
IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes to 2 hours; non-IgE (FPIES, proctocolitis) are delayed.
Sensitisation on SPT or IgE is not allergy; history is key; oral food challenge is the gold standard.
Introduce allergenic foods including peanut and egg in the first year, around 6 months, and keep them in the diet.
Red ASCIA plan with autoinjector for anaphylaxis risk; green plan for allergic reactions.
Milk allergy: extensively hydrolysed formula first; amino acid formula if severe.
Milk and egg allergy usually resolve; peanut, tree nut and seafood allergies usually persist.
redFlags: Previous anaphylaxis
Food allergy with poorly controlled asthma
Peanut or tree nut allergy in an adolescent (higher fatality risk)
Food bolus impaction or dysphagia (eosinophilic oesophagitis)

contrast.india: Advice to delay egg, nuts and fish is still common among families.
contrast.australia: ASCIA: introduce peanut and egg in the first year, around 6 months (not before 4 months).

contrast.india: Broad IgE panels ordered without history in private labs.
contrast.australia: Test only for foods suggested by history; oral food challenge by specialists; unproven tests discouraged.

flashcards.front: ASCIA advice on timing of solids?
flashcards.back: Around 6 months, not before 4 months, when developmentally ready.

flashcards.front: When should peanut and egg be introduced to infants?
flashcards.back: In the first year of life, then given regularly.

flashcards.front: First-line formula for cow's milk protein allergy?
flashcards.back: Extensively hydrolysed formula (amino acid formula if severe).

flashcards.front: Gold standard test for food allergy?
flashcards.back: Supervised oral food challenge.

flashcards.front: Classic presentation of FPIES?
flashcards.back: Repetitive profuse vomiting 1-4 hours after a trigger food, with pallor and lethargy, no skin or respiratory signs.

quiz.stem: A mother brings her 5-month-old daughter, who has moderate eczema, to discuss starting solids. Her older son has peanut allergy and she plans to avoid peanut and egg until her daughter is 3 years old. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Avoid peanut and egg until 3 years of age
Start solids now and introduce peanut and egg later in the second year
Arrange skin prick testing to all common food allergens before any solids are introduced
Introduce solids around 6 months, including peanut and well-cooked egg in the first year, and continue them regularly, while treating the eczema
Switch to a partially hydrolysed formula to prevent allergy
quiz.explanation:
ASCIA recommends that **all infants**, including those at higher risk (eczema, sibling with allergy), start solids **around 6 months (not before 4 months)** and have common allergenic foods, including **smooth peanut and well-cooked egg, introduced in the first year of life**, then **given regularly**.

Delaying allergenic foods **increases** the risk of food allergy (as shown by the LEAP trial for peanut). Active **eczema treatment** matters because inflamed skin is a route for sensitisation. Routine screening tests before introduction are not recommended for most infants, and hydrolysed formulas are no longer recommended for allergy prevention.
whyWrong: Delaying allergenic foods increases the risk of allergy.
Introduction should occur in the first year, not the second.
Routine screening before introduction is not recommended and causes false positives.
Partially hydrolysed formula does not prevent allergy.

quiz.stem: A 6-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after three episodes of profuse, repetitive vomiting starting 2 hours after her first taste of rice cereal. She is pale and lethargic, but has no rash, wheeze or swelling. HR 170/min, capillary refill 3 seconds. This happened once before with the same food. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: IgE-mediated rice allergy with anaphylaxis
Food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome (FPIES)
Viral gastroenteritis
Pyloric stenosis
Coeliac disease
quiz.explanation:
**FPIES** is a non-IgE-mediated food allergy that presents with **repetitive, profuse vomiting 1-4 hours after ingestion**, with **pallor and lethargy**, sometimes progressing to hypotension. There are **no skin or respiratory features**. Common triggers in Australia include **rice**, cow's milk, egg and oats. Recurrence with the same food supports the diagnosis.

Treatment is **fluid resuscitation** (IV if dehydrated or shocked); ondansetron may help. Adrenaline and antihistamines do not help because it is not IgE-mediated. Skin prick tests are usually negative. The food is avoided and a specialist arranges a supervised challenge later, as most children outgrow it.
whyWrong: IgE-mediated reactions occur sooner and usually involve skin or respiratory signs.
Gastroenteritis would not reproducibly follow one food, and diarrhoea usually follows.
Pyloric stenosis occurs at 2-8 weeks with projectile vomiting after every feed.
Coeliac disease causes chronic symptoms, not acute vomiting after a first exposure.

quiz.stem: A 7-year-old boy has a skin prick test that shows a 5 mm wheal to egg, ordered by another doctor as part of a panel for his eczema. He has eaten scrambled egg and cakes regularly for years without any symptoms. His mother asks whether he should stop eating egg. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Stop all egg and prescribe an adrenaline autoinjector
Stop all egg until an oral food challenge can be arranged
Continue eating egg as usual; the test shows sensitisation, not allergy
Repeat the skin prick test in 6 months
Avoid raw egg only and give a green ASCIA action plan
quiz.explanation:
A positive skin prick test or specific IgE shows **sensitisation**, not clinical allergy. The diagnosis of food allergy needs a **history of reactions** on exposure. A child who **regularly eats a food without symptoms is tolerant**, and stopping it could actually lead to loss of tolerance and true allergy.

This is why ASCIA advises against **testing without a relevant history** (broad panels): false positives lead to unnecessary avoidance and nutritional problems. He should keep eating egg regularly.
whyWrong: He has no clinical allergy; an autoinjector and avoidance are not indicated.
A food challenge is unnecessary when he already tolerates egg regularly.
Repeat testing adds nothing; tolerance is already demonstrated.
No action plan is needed without a history of reactions.

lessons.title: Type 1 diabetes and childhood obesity
objectives: Recognise new type 1 diabetes early and arrange same-day assessment
Outline insulin regimens, hypoglycaemia treatment, sick-day rules and school support in Australia
Assess childhood overweight and obesity with BMI-for-age centiles and screen for complications
Distinguish type 2 from type 1 diabetes in young people and plan family-based lifestyle management

sections.heading: Two metabolic problems of Australian childhood
sections.body:
**Type 1 diabetes (T1D)** is one of the commonest serious chronic diseases of childhood; Australia has one of the higher incidences worldwide. About a third of children are in **DKA at diagnosis**, and DKA is more common in younger children because early symptoms are missed. The "**4Ts**" campaign (Toilet, Thirsty, Tired, Thinner) promotes early testing.

**Obesity** affects many more children: about **1 in 4 Australian children** aged 2-17 is overweight or obese. It tracks into adulthood and brings early complications, including **type 2 diabetes in adolescents**, which is increasing, especially in **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander** young people and those of South Asian, Pacific Islander and Middle Eastern background.

sections.heading: Type 1 diabetes: presentation and diagnosis
sections.body:
**Pathogenesis**: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells in a genetically susceptible child (HLA-DR3/DR4). Autoantibodies (**GAD, IA-2, ZnT8, insulin**) appear months to years before symptoms. Symptoms appear when most beta-cell function is lost.

**Symptoms**: **polyuria** (including **new bedwetting** in a previously dry child), **polydipsia**, **weight loss**, tiredness, irritability, oral or genital thrush. In DKA: vomiting, abdominal pain, deep sighing breathing, drowsiness.

**Diagnosis in a symptomatic child**: a **random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more** with symptoms, supported by **ketones**. The critical action: **a child with suggestive symptoms needs a finger-prick glucose (and ketones) the same day**, and if positive, **same-day referral** to a paediatric emergency department or diabetes team. Do **not** send them for a fasting glucose or oral glucose tolerance test the next week, which delays diagnosis while the child slides into DKA.

At diagnosis, children are also screened for associated autoimmune disease: **coeliac disease** (tTG-IgA with total IgA) and **thyroid disease** (TSH, thyroid antibodies), then periodically.

sections.heading: Type 1 diabetes: long-term care
sections.body:
Care is led by a **paediatric multidisciplinary diabetes team** (paediatric endocrinologist, diabetes educator, dietitian, psychologist, social worker).

**Insulin regimens**
- **Multiple daily injections (basal-bolus)**: long-acting basal insulin once daily plus rapid-acting insulin with meals, dosed by carbohydrate counting.
- **Insulin pump therapy** (continuous subcutaneous insulin), increasingly with **hybrid closed-loop** systems linked to a CGM.
- **Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM)** is subsidised through the **National Diabetes Services Scheme (NDSS)** for people with type 1 diabetes (eligibility details on the NDSS site). Most Australian children use CGM.

**Targets**: HbA1c around **7% (53 mmol/mol) or lower**, individualised, and time in range on CGM, while minimising hypoglycaemia.

**Hypoglycaemia** (glucose under 4.0 mmol/L):
- Conscious and able to swallow: **fast-acting carbohydrate** (glucose tablets, jelly beans, juice) in an age-appropriate amount, recheck in 15 minutes, repeat if still low, then a longer-acting carbohydrate if the next meal is not due.
- Unconscious, seizing or unable to swallow: **do not give anything by mouth**. Give **glucagon IM** (0.5 mg for children under about 25 kg, 1 mg for heavier children, per product information) or intranasal glucagon where available, or IV glucose in hospital (10% glucose 2 mL/kg).

**Sick-day rules**: **never stop insulin** (illness usually increases insulin needs); check glucose and **blood ketones** every 2-4 hours; extra rapid-acting insulin per the team's plan; maintain fluids; **seek urgent help** if ketones are rising, vomiting persists, or the child is drowsy or breathing deeply.

**School and daily life**: a **diabetes management plan** and **action plan** for school, trained staff, access to hypo treatment; exercise causes hypoglycaemia (including delayed overnight). The **honeymoon period** after diagnosis (partial beta-cell recovery, low insulin needs) can last months.

**Complication screening** from puberty or after a few years of diabetes (per national guidelines): retinopathy, microalbuminuria, blood pressure, lipids, thyroid, coeliac, feet. **Adolescence** brings worsening control (insulin resistance of puberty, risk-taking, eating disorders, adherence) and needs a planned **transition** to adult services. Mental health screening matters.

sections.heading: Childhood obesity: assessment
sections.body:
**Measuring**: plot **BMI-for-age** on growth charts (CDC charts are commonly used in Australia for 2-18 years; WHO charts under 2).
- **Overweight**: BMI at or above the **85th** centile
- **Obesity**: at or above the **95th** centile

**Causes**: overwhelmingly **environmental and behavioural** (energy-dense food, sugary drinks, screen time, reduced activity, short sleep) on a background of genetic susceptibility. Look for rare causes when:

| Clue | Consider |
|---|---|
| **Short stature or falling height velocity** with weight gain | **Endocrine**: hypothyroidism, Cushing syndrome (including iatrogenic steroids), growth hormone deficiency. Simple obesity usually makes children **taller** |
| Severe obesity before age 5, hyperphagia, developmental delay, dysmorphism | **Genetic**: Prader-Willi syndrome, MC4R and leptin pathway defects |
| Medications | Antipsychotics (risperidone), corticosteroids, some anticonvulsants |

**Screen for complications**:
- **Obstructive sleep apnoea** (snoring, pauses, daytime sleepiness, behaviour problems)
- **Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD)**: raised ALT
- **Insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes**: **acanthosis nigricans**, HbA1c or fasting glucose
- **Hypertension** (use appropriately sized cuff and centile tables), **dyslipidaemia**
- **Slipped capital femoral epiphysis** (hip or knee pain, limp), Blount disease
- **Idiopathic intracranial hypertension** (headache, papilloedema)
- **PCOS** in adolescent girls
- **Psychosocial**: bullying, low self-esteem, depression, disordered eating

sections.heading: Obesity and type 2 diabetes: management
sections.body:
**Family-based lifestyle change** is the foundation (Australian clinical practice guidelines for overweight and obesity in children, and RACGP guidance):
- Involve the **whole family**; parents are the agents of change for younger children.
- Use **non-stigmatising language** ("healthy weight", "growing into their weight").
- Aim for **weight maintenance or slowed gain in growing children** (so BMI centile falls with height gain), and gradual weight loss in adolescents or severe obesity.
- **Diet**: water instead of sugary drinks, regular family meals, portion sizes, fruit and vegetables, fewer discretionary foods. Avoid restrictive diets in young children.
- **Activity**: Australian guidelines recommend at least **60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily** for children 5-17, and limiting recreational screen time.
- **Sleep**: age-appropriate sleep duration.
- Programs, dietitians and psychologists as needed; referral to a paediatric weight management service for severe obesity or complications.
- **Pharmacotherapy** (for example GLP-1 receptor agonists) and **bariatric surgery** are specialist options for adolescents with severe obesity.

**Type 2 diabetes in youth**
- Suspect in an adolescent with obesity, **acanthosis nigricans**, family history, or high-risk ethnicity (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, South Asian, Pacific Islander).
- Usually no or mild ketosis at diagnosis (but DKA can occur), **negative islet autoantibodies**, and preserved C-peptide.
- Management: lifestyle plus **metformin** first line; insulin if very high glucose, ketosis or HbA1c markedly raised. Complications appear faster than in adult-onset disease, and early screening for nephropathy and hypertension is needed.

| Feature | Type 1 | Type 2 (youth) |
|---|---|---|
| Onset | Any age, often abrupt | Puberty or later, insidious |
| Body habitus | Usually normal/thin | Obese |
| Acanthosis nigricans | Uncommon | Common |
| Ketosis/DKA | Common | Less common |
| Autoantibodies | Positive | Negative |
| Treatment | Insulin always | Lifestyle, metformin, +/- insulin |

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Child with polyuria, weight loss and new bedwetting: **same-day finger-prick glucose and ketones**, then same-day referral. Choosing "fasting glucose next week" is wrong.
- Unconscious child with diabetes: **glucagon IM**, never oral glucose.
- Sick child with T1D who isn't eating: **continue insulin**, check ketones.
- New T1D: screen for **coeliac and thyroid disease**.
- Obese child who is **short**: look for an endocrine cause. Obese child who is **tall**: simple obesity.
- Obese adolescent with acanthosis nigricans: screen for **type 2 diabetes**; metformin first line.
- Obesity management: **family-based**, weight maintenance while growing.

keyPoints: Symptoms of T1D (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, new bedwetting) need same-day glucose and ketone testing.
Screen new T1D for coeliac and thyroid disease.
Hypoglycaemia under 4.0 mmol/L: fast-acting carbohydrate; if unconscious, glucagon IM, nothing by mouth.
Sick days: never stop insulin; check ketones; seek help if ketones rise or vomiting persists.
CGM is NDSS-subsidised; school diabetes management plans are standard.
Overweight at or above the 85th BMI centile, obesity at or above the 95th.
Obesity with short stature suggests an endocrine cause; screen for OSA, fatty liver, T2D and hypertension.
Obesity: family-based lifestyle change; T2D in youth: lifestyle plus metformin.
redFlags: Polyuria, weight loss and vomiting (possible DKA)
Deep sighing respiration in a child with diabetes
Unconscious or seizing child with diabetes
Obesity with short stature or falling height velocity
Obese child with limp or knee pain (SCFE)
Headache and visual symptoms in an obese adolescent (IIH)

contrast.india: Finger-prick testing, often limited by cost.
contrast.australia: Subsidised CGM through the NDSS is standard for most children; pumps and closed-loop systems common.

contrast.india: Undernutrition remains the dominant concern; obesity rising in urban children.
contrast.australia: About 1 in 4 children overweight or obese; BMI-for-age centiles and family-based management in general practice.

flashcards.front: Glucose threshold for diabetes in a symptomatic child?
flashcards.back: Random glucose of 11.1 mmol/L or more.

flashcards.front: Autoimmune conditions to screen for at T1D diagnosis?
flashcards.back: Coeliac disease (tTG-IgA with total IgA) and thyroid disease.

flashcards.front: Treatment of severe hypoglycaemia in an unconscious child at home?
flashcards.back: Glucagon IM (0.5 mg if under about 25 kg, 1 mg if heavier); nothing by mouth.

flashcards.front: BMI-for-age centile defining obesity in children?
flashcards.back: 95th centile or above (overweight 85th or above).

flashcards.front: Skin sign of insulin resistance?
flashcards.back: Acanthosis nigricans.

flashcards.front: First-line drug for type 2 diabetes in adolescents?
flashcards.back: Metformin (with lifestyle change).

quiz.stem: A 6-year-old girl is brought to her GP because she has started wetting the bed again after being dry for 2 years. Her mother says she is drinking a lot and seems tired, and her clothes are looser. She is alert, with normal vital signs. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Send urine for microscopy and culture and review in 3 days
Arrange a fasting glucose at the pathology lab tomorrow
Check a finger-prick blood glucose and ketones in the clinic today
Reassure and start a bedwetting alarm
Arrange an oral glucose tolerance test
quiz.explanation:
**Secondary enuresis, polydipsia, tiredness and weight loss** in a child are the classic symptoms of **type 1 diabetes** (the 4Ts: toilet, thirsty, tired, thinner). The critical step is a **same-day finger-prick glucose and ketone test** in the clinic. If the glucose is high, she needs **same-day referral** to a paediatric emergency department or diabetes team.

Children can progress to **DKA within hours to days**; delays for fasting glucose, an OGTT or a urine culture are a common cause of preventable DKA. A UTI can cause secondary enuresis, but it does not explain polydipsia and weight loss.
whyWrong: Waiting for a urine culture delays diagnosis of likely diabetes.
A fasting test tomorrow delays diagnosis and risks DKA.
Missing diabetes is dangerous; enuresis here is a symptom of polyuria.
An OGTT is not needed in a symptomatic child and delays care.
quiz.ausPearl: Australian campaigns promote the 4Ts (Toilet, Thirsty, Tired, Thinner) to reduce DKA at diagnosis.

quiz.stem: A 12-year-old boy (35 kg) with type 1 diabetes is found by his mother unrousable in bed in the morning. He is breathing normally. His CGM reads 1.9 mmol/L. She has his diabetes kit at home. What is the most appropriate immediate action by the mother?
options: Give him orange juice to drink
Give his usual morning insulin dose
Rub honey on his gums and wait 30 minutes
Put him in the recovery position, give glucagon 1 mg IM and call an ambulance
Give him glucose tablets
quiz.explanation:
This is **severe hypoglycaemia** (unrousable), so nothing should be given by mouth because of the risk of **aspiration**. The treatment at home is **glucagon IM** (1 mg for children over about 25 kg; 0.5 mg for smaller children), or intranasal glucagon where prescribed, with the child in the **recovery position** and an ambulance called.

Once he wakes and can swallow, give fast-acting then longer-acting carbohydrate, as glucagon's effect is short and nausea is common. Afterwards, the team should review the cause (for example exercise the day before, an insulin error, or alcohol in an adolescent) and adjust the plan.
whyWrong: Oral fluids risk aspiration in an unconscious child.
Insulin would worsen the hypoglycaemia.
Buccal honey is not reliable and delays effective treatment.
Tablets cannot be safely swallowed by an unconscious child.

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought in because of weight gain over 2 years. His BMI is above the 97th centile. His height has dropped from the 50th to the 10th centile over the same period. He has red-purple striae and a round face. He has not been on steroid medication. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure and start a family-based lifestyle program only
Refer to a dietitian and review in 12 months
Start metformin
Arrange a sleep study
Investigate for an endocrine cause, such as Cushing syndrome, with paediatric endocrinology referral
quiz.explanation:
Children with simple (nutritional) obesity are usually **tall for their age**, because excess nutrition accelerates growth. **Weight gain with falling height velocity** points to an **endocrine cause**: **Cushing syndrome**, hypothyroidism or growth hormone deficiency. Purple striae and a round face strengthen the suspicion of cortisol excess.

After excluding exogenous steroids (including inhaled, topical and nasal), he needs **referral to a paediatric endocrinologist** for investigations (for example late-night salivary cortisol or 24-hour urinary free cortisol, dexamethasone suppression), plus thyroid function. Lifestyle advice alone would miss a treatable cause.
whyWrong: Growth failure with obesity is not simple obesity and needs investigation.
Waiting 12 months delays diagnosis of a likely endocrine cause.
Metformin does not address the underlying cause.
OSA screening may be relevant but is not the priority here.

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old girl with type 1 diabetes on multiple daily injections has gastroenteritis. She has vomited twice today and is eating very little. Her mother stopped her insulin this morning 'because she isn't eating'. Glucose is 16 mmol/L and blood ketones are 1.8 mmol/L. She is alert and drinking small amounts. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Keep insulin stopped until she is eating normally

Give her basal insulin as usual plus extra rapid-acting insulin per her sick-day plan, check glucose and ketones every 2 hours, maintain fluids, and seek urgent review if ketones rise or vomiting continues
Give only half her basal insulin and recheck tomorrow
Give oral rehydration solution only and no insulin
Give a full meal dose of rapid-acting insulin and check again tomorrow
quiz.explanation:
The key **sick-day rule** is **never stop insulin**. Illness raises counter-regulatory hormones, so insulin requirements usually **increase**, and without insulin the body makes ketones and heads toward **DKA**. Her ketones of 1.8 mmol/L are already raised.

She should have her **usual basal insulin**, **extra rapid-acting insulin** as directed by her diabetes team's sick-day plan, **frequent glucose and ketone checks**, and fluids (with carbohydrate if glucose falls). The family should call the diabetes team, and go to hospital if ketones keep rising, vomiting persists or she becomes drowsy or breathless.
whyWrong: Stopping insulin leads to ketosis and DKA.
Reducing basal insulin with rising ketones is unsafe, and checking tomorrow is far too late.
Fluids alone will not stop ketone production.
A single large dose without monitoring risks hypoglycaemia and misses rising ketones.

lessons.title: Epilepsy in children
objectives: Define epilepsy and investigate a first unprovoked seizure appropriately
Recognise the common childhood epilepsy syndromes from their description
Match first-line drugs to syndromes and avoid drugs that worsen specific epilepsies
Counsel families on safety, school, seizure plans and valproate in girls

sections.heading: Epilepsy in the Australian child
sections.body:
Epilepsy affects about **1 in 200** children. Most are managed by paediatricians or paediatric neurologists, with GPs coordinating care, prescriptions and school plans. The AMC mostly tests **syndrome recognition** from a description (often including an EEG phrase), **first-line drug choice**, and **safety counselling**.

**Definition (ILAE)**: two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart; or one unprovoked seizure with a high (at least 60%) risk of recurrence (for example with an epileptiform EEG or structural brain lesion); or diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome. Febrile seizures and provoked seizures (hypoglycaemia, head injury) are not epilepsy.

sections.heading: After a first afebrile seizure
sections.body:
- **Detailed history**, ideally with a witness and **video** on a phone: what happened before (trigger, aura), during (onset focal or generalised, duration), and after (post-ictal state, Todd paresis). Many "seizures" are syncope, breath-holding or other mimics.
- **Glucose and electrolytes** acutely; **ECG** if there is any suggestion of syncope or cardiac cause (long QT can present as "seizures", especially with exercise, swimming or startle).
- **EEG**: helps classify the seizure type and epilepsy syndrome and predicts recurrence. A normal interictal EEG does not exclude epilepsy. Sleep-deprived EEG increases yield.
- **MRI brain** for focal seizures, abnormal neurological examination, developmental delay, or seizures in infancy. Not needed for classic generalised syndromes like childhood absence epilepsy.
- **Treatment is not usually started after a single unprovoked seizure**; the decision is made with a specialist based on recurrence risk.

sections.heading: Common childhood epilepsy syndromes
sections.body:
| Syndrome | Age and features | EEG | First-line treatment |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Infantile spasms (infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, West syndrome)** | **3-12 months**; clusters of sudden flexion (or extension) spasms, often on waking; **developmental regression**; causes include **tuberous sclerosis** | **Hypsarrhythmia** | **Urgent** referral: prednisolone/ACTH or **vigabatrin** (first choice in tuberous sclerosis) |
| **Dravet syndrome** | Infancy; prolonged, often hemiclonic **febrile seizures** from about 6 months, then multiple seizure types and developmental slowing; **SCN1A** mutation | Normal early | Valproate, clobazam, stiripentol, fenfluramine, cannabidiol (specialist). **Avoid sodium channel blockers** (carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin) |
| **Childhood absence epilepsy** | **4-10 years**, more in girls; many brief (seconds) staring spells a day, abrupt start and stop, no post-ictal state; teachers report "daydreaming"; **triggered by hyperventilation** | **3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave** | **Ethosuximide** (valproate or lamotrigine alternatives) |
| **Self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes** (benign rolandic) | **3-13 years**; seizures from sleep; one-sided facial twitching, drooling, gurgling, speech arrest, may generalise | Centrotemporal spikes | Often **no treatment**; remits by adolescence |
| **Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy** | **Adolescence**; **morning myoclonic jerks** (drops things at breakfast), generalised tonic-clonic seizures, absences; triggered by **sleep deprivation and alcohol** | Generalised polyspike-and-wave, photosensitivity | Valproate is effective but avoid in females who could become pregnant; **levetiracetam** or lamotrigine often used. Lifelong tendency |
| **Lennox-Gastaut syndrome** | Early childhood; multiple seizure types including tonic and atonic ("drop attacks"), intellectual disability | Slow spike-and-wave | Specialist; often drug-resistant |

**Drugs that worsen specific epilepsies**: **carbamazepine** (and other sodium channel blockers) can aggravate **absence and myoclonic** seizures and Dravet syndrome.

sections.heading: Treatment principles and counselling
sections.body:
**Medication**: start one drug at a low dose and titrate (monotherapy controls most). About two-thirds of children become seizure-free. **Drug-resistant epilepsy** (failure of two appropriate drugs) should be referred to a comprehensive epilepsy centre for consideration of **surgery**, **ketogenic diet**, or vagus nerve stimulation.

**Common side effects to know**
- **Sodium valproate**: weight gain, tremor, hair loss, hepatotoxicity (especially under 2 years and with metabolic disease), pancreatitis, and **high teratogenicity** (neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental problems). It is avoided in girls and women who could become pregnant unless there is no alternative, with a pregnancy prevention plan (TGA warnings).
- **Carbamazepine**: rash (HLA-B*1502 association with Stevens-Johnson syndrome in people of Han Chinese, Thai and some other Asian ancestry), hyponatraemia, enzyme induction.
- **Lamotrigine**: rash (titrate slowly, especially with valproate).
- **Levetiracetam**: irritability, behavioural and mood change.
- **Ethosuximide**: GI upset.

**Safety and life**
- **Showers instead of baths**, or supervised bathing; **swimming only with close supervision** (drowning risk is much higher).
- Avoid unsupervised heights, cycling with helmet in safe areas.
- **Seizure management plan** for school and home, often including **buccal or intranasal midazolam** for seizures lasting 5 minutes (see paediatric emergencies).
- **SUDEP** (sudden unexpected death in epilepsy) is rare in children but real; risk is higher with frequent uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures. Discuss in a balanced way.
- **Driving** for adolescents: Austroads "Assessing Fitness to Drive" sets seizure-free periods before licensing; check the current standard.
- Adolescents: sleep hygiene, alcohol, contraception interactions (enzyme inducers reduce hormonal contraceptive efficacy), and planned transition.
- School performance, learning and mental health support (anxiety and depression are more common).
- Stopping medication: often considered after about **2 seizure-free years**, with specialist guidance, depending on syndrome.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Brief staring many times a day in a 7-year-old, provoked by hyperventilation, **3 Hz spike-wave**: **childhood absence epilepsy, ethosuximide**.
- Morning jerks in a teenager who drops her cereal spoon: **JME**; avoid carbamazepine; think carefully before valproate in a girl.
- Nocturnal facial twitching and drooling in a school-aged child with centrotemporal spikes: **self-limited (rolandic) epilepsy**, often no treatment.
- Clusters of spasms and regression in a 6-month-old: **infantile spasms**, urgent referral. Look for ash-leaf macules (tuberous sclerosis).
- Prolonged febrile seizures in infancy with later developmental problems: **Dravet**, avoid sodium channel blockers.
- "Seizure" during exercise or swimming: get an **ECG** (long QT).
- Showers not baths; supervised swimming.
- Seizure first aid for families and teachers: time it, protect from injury, nothing in the mouth, recovery position once jerking stops, call an ambulance at 5 minutes or if injured, in water, or not recovering.
- A child with epilepsy who is doing badly at school: think frequent absences, drug side effects (sedation, behaviour change with levetiracetam), comorbid ADHD or learning disorder, or low mood.

keyPoints: Epilepsy: two unprovoked seizures over 24 hours apart, or one with at least 60% recurrence risk, or a syndrome.
After a first seizure: history with video, glucose, ECG if cardiac possible, EEG; MRI if focal or in infancy.
Childhood absence epilepsy: 3 Hz spike-wave, hyperventilation-provoked; ethosuximide first line.
Infantile spasms: hypsarrhythmia and regression; urgent referral; vigabatrin in tuberous sclerosis.
JME: morning myoclonus in adolescence; avoid carbamazepine; valproate avoided in girls who could become pregnant.
Carbamazepine worsens absence and myoclonic seizures; sodium channel blockers worsen Dravet syndrome.
Safety: showers, supervised swimming, seizure management plan with midazolam.
redFlags: Developmental regression with spasms in an infant
Focal seizures or abnormal neurological examination
Seizures triggered by exercise, swimming or startle (think long QT)
Seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer
Frequent uncontrolled tonic-clonic seizures (SUDEP risk)

contrast.india: Valproate is widely prescribed as a cheap broad-spectrum drug for all.
contrast.australia: Avoided in girls and women who could become pregnant unless no alternative, with a pregnancy prevention plan (TGA).

contrast.india: Families often have no written plan or rescue medication.
contrast.australia: Written seizure management plans for school, with buccal or intranasal midazolam for prolonged seizures.

flashcards.back: 3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave, provoked by hyperventilation.

flashcards.back: Hypsarrhythmia.

flashcards.back: Vigabatrin.

flashcards.back: Sodium channel blockers: carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin.
