flashcards.back: High teratogenicity (neural tube defects, neurodevelopmental harm).

quiz.stem: A 7-year-old girl's teacher reports that she 'zones out' many times a day for a few seconds, stopping mid-sentence and then carrying on as if nothing happened. In the clinic, asking her to breathe fast for 2 minutes triggers a 10-second episode of staring and eyelid fluttering. She is otherwise well with normal development. EEG shows generalised 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Carbamazepine
Ethosuximide
Phenytoin
Vigabatrin
No treatment; reassure
quiz.explanation:
Brief, frequent staring spells with abrupt onset and offset, **no post-ictal state**, provoked by **hyperventilation**, and **3 Hz generalised spike-and-wave** on EEG are diagnostic of **childhood absence epilepsy**. First-line treatment is **ethosuximide**; valproate and lamotrigine are alternatives (valproate being less preferred in girls because of teratogenicity later).

Treatment matters because frequent absences impair learning and safety. **Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen absence seizures**. Most children remit by adolescence.
whyWrong: Carbamazepine can aggravate absence seizures.
Phenytoin is ineffective and can worsen absences.
Vigabatrin is for infantile spasms and can worsen absences.
Frequent absences affect learning and safety and should be treated.

quiz.stem: A 6-month-old boy has had episodes over 2 weeks in which he suddenly flexes his trunk and throws his arms forward, several times in a row, especially on waking. He has stopped smiling and no longer reaches for toys. On examination there are several hypopigmented oval macules on his trunk. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure the parents that this is colic
Start a trial of reflux medication
Review in 3 months to monitor development
Urgent referral to a paediatric neurologist for EEG and treatment
Arrange a hearing test
quiz.explanation:
Clusters of **flexor spasms on waking** with **developmental regression** in an infant are **infantile spasms (West syndrome)**. The hypopigmented **ash-leaf macules** suggest **tuberous sclerosis**, a common underlying cause.

This is an **epileptic emergency**: the EEG typically shows **hypsarrhythmia**, and delay in treatment worsens developmental outcome. He needs **urgent referral** (days, not months) for EEG, MRI and treatment, with **vigabatrin** first choice in tuberous sclerosis (steroids or ACTH in other causes).
whyWrong: Colic doesn't cause stereotyped spasms or regression.
Reflux (Sandifer) causes arching after feeds, not clusters on waking with regression.
Delay worsens developmental outcome.
Hearing loss doesn't explain the spasms or skin findings.

quiz.stem: A 15-year-old girl had a generalised tonic-clonic seizure at a sleepover after staying up all night. Her mother says that for months she has had sudden jerks of her arms in the mornings, sometimes dropping her toothbrush or spilling her drink. EEG shows generalised polyspike-and-wave discharges with photosensitivity. Which medication is most appropriate to start, in discussion with a neurologist?
options: Carbamazepine
Sodium valproate as first choice without further discussion
Phenytoin
Ethosuximide alone
Levetiracetam
quiz.explanation:
**Morning myoclonic jerks**, a tonic-clonic seizure after **sleep deprivation**, and generalised polyspike-and-wave with photosensitivity in an adolescent are **juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME)**.

Valproate is very effective for JME, but it is **highly teratogenic**, and TGA guidance is to avoid it in girls and women who could become pregnant unless other options fail, with a pregnancy prevention plan. **Levetiracetam** (or lamotrigine) is a common first choice in adolescent girls. **Carbamazepine and phenytoin can worsen myoclonic seizures**, and ethosuximide doesn't control tonic-clonic seizures.

Counsel about sleep, alcohol, driving rules and the usually lifelong nature of JME.
whyWrong: Carbamazepine can aggravate myoclonic seizures and absences.
Valproate's teratogenicity means it should not be started in a teenage girl without careful discussion of alternatives.
Phenytoin can worsen myoclonic seizures.
Ethosuximide does not control generalised tonic-clonic seizures.

lessons.title: Cystic fibrosis
objectives: Explain how CFTR dysfunction produces the lung, pancreatic and sweat features of CF
Follow the newborn screening pathway to a confirmatory sweat chloride test
Outline multidisciplinary CF management, including CFTR modulators on the PBS
Counsel families on inheritance and carrier screening

sections.heading: CF in Australia
sections.body:
Cystic fibrosis is the most common life-limiting **autosomal recessive** condition in people of European ancestry. In Australia about **1 in 25** people of European background are carriers, and roughly **1 in 2,500-3,500 babies** are born with CF. Every Australian newborn is screened for CF through the **newborn bloodspot (heel prick) screening** program, so most children are diagnosed in the first weeks of life before symptoms. Survival has improved dramatically; many people with CF now live into middle age and beyond, and **CFTR modulators** are changing the outlook again.

CF is managed in **specialist CF centres** with a multidisciplinary team.

sections.heading: From one gene to many organs
sections.body:
**CFTR** (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator) is a chloride and bicarbonate channel on epithelial surfaces, encoded on **chromosome 7**. The commonest mutation is **F508del** (misfolded protein that doesn't reach the cell surface). Loss of CFTR function causes:

- **Airways**: reduced chloride secretion and increased sodium absorption dehydrate the airway surface liquid; mucus becomes thick and mucociliary clearance fails. This leads to chronic infection (early **Staphylococcus aureus** and **Haemophilus influenzae**, later **Pseudomonas aeruginosa**, and others such as Burkholderia cepacia complex and non-tuberculous mycobacteria), neutrophilic inflammation and **bronchiectasis**. Upper airway: chronic sinusitis, **nasal polyps**.
- **Pancreas**: thick secretions block ducts, causing **exocrine pancreatic insufficiency** in most (malabsorption of fat and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, K) and later **CF-related diabetes**.
- **Gut**: **meconium ileus** in newborns (about 10-20%), **distal intestinal obstruction syndrome (DIOS)** in older patients, rectal prolapse.
- **Liver**: focal biliary cirrhosis, gallstones.
- **Sweat glands**: CFTR normally reabsorbs chloride from sweat, so sweat is **salty**. This is the basis of the sweat test, and the reason for **salt depletion in hot weather** (hyponatraemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis: a real risk in Australian summers).
- **Reproductive**: **congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens** (almost all males are infertile but can father children with assisted reproduction); reduced fertility in females (thick cervical mucus).

sections.heading: Newborn screening and diagnosis
sections.body:
**Newborn bloodspot screening**: heel prick sample at **48-72 hours**. The screening pathway measures **immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT)**, which is raised in CF because pancreatic duct obstruction pushes trypsinogen into the blood, followed by **DNA testing for common CFTR mutations** on high IRT samples. A positive screen is **not a diagnosis**: the baby is referred to a CF centre.

**Sweat chloride test** (pilocarpine iontophoresis) confirms the diagnosis:

| Sweat chloride | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **60 mmol/L or more** | **Consistent with CF** |
| 30-59 mmol/L | Intermediate: further testing (extended genetics) |
| Under 30 mmol/L | CF unlikely |

Two disease-causing CFTR mutations also support the diagnosis. The sweat test is done once the baby is over about 2 weeks and 2 kg (enough sweat).

**Screening is not perfect**: rare mutations can be missed. **A child with symptoms suggestive of CF needs a sweat test even if the newborn screen was negative** (or was done overseas, or not done). Presentations to remember: failure to thrive with **greasy, pale, offensive stools** and a big appetite, recurrent chest infections or chronic wet cough, **nasal polyps in a child**, rectal prolapse, meconium ileus, and hyponatraemic dehydration in heat.

**Other tests**: faecal elastase (low in pancreatic insufficiency), sputum or cough swab cultures, chest imaging, spirometry from school age, fat-soluble vitamin levels, and annual oral glucose tolerance testing from around age 10 for CF-related diabetes.

sections.heading: Multidisciplinary care
sections.body:
**Respiratory**
- **Daily airway clearance** physiotherapy (techniques and devices appropriate to age) and exercise.
- Mucoactive agents: **dornase alfa**, **hypertonic saline**.
- **Antibiotics** for exacerbations (oral or IV "tune-ups"); regular surveillance cultures.
- **Pseudomonas eradication** at first isolation (for example inhaled tobramycin), and inhaled antibiotics for chronic infection.
- Some Australian centres use anti-staphylococcal prophylaxis (flucloxacillin) in young children; practice varies by centre.
- **Infection control**: people with CF should not mix closely with each other (cross-infection with resistant organisms); CF clinics segregate patients.
- Annual influenza vaccine plus the routine schedule.
- Lung transplantation for end-stage disease.

**Nutrition and gastrointestinal**
- **Pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy** with every meal and snack containing fat.
- **High-energy, high-fat diet**; **fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K**.
- **Salt supplements**, especially for infants and in hot weather.
- Manage DIOS (laxatives, fluids), monitor liver disease, screen for **CF-related diabetes**.

**CFTR modulators**
- These drugs correct or potentiate the faulty CFTR protein. The triple combination **elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor** improves lung function, weight and sweat chloride dramatically in people with at least one F508del mutation. Modulators are **PBS-subsidised for eligible patients**, with age and genotype criteria that have been expanding (check the current PBS listing).
- Monitor liver function and eye checks (cataracts in children) as advised.

**Psychosocial and transition**: heavy treatment burden, adherence in adolescence, mental health, and transition to adult CF services.

sections.heading: Genetic counselling
sections.body:
- Both parents of an affected child are (almost always) carriers. Each pregnancy has a **1 in 4** chance of an affected child, **1 in 2** chance of a carrier, and **1 in 4** chance of neither.
- An unaffected sibling of a child with CF has a **2 in 3** chance of being a carrier.
- **Reproductive carrier screening** for CF, spinal muscular atrophy and fragile X is recommended to be offered to all people planning pregnancy or in early pregnancy (RANZCOG, RACGP), and has a Medicare rebate.
- Couples who are both carriers can consider prenatal diagnosis (CVS or amniocentesis) or preimplantation genetic testing with IVF.
- Carriers are healthy; a positive newborn screen that turns out to be a carrier result is an opportunity to offer testing to the parents and extended family.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Positive newborn screen: **next step is a sweat chloride test** at a CF centre (60 mmol/L or more confirms).
- Failure to thrive, steatorrhoea and recurrent chest infections in a child who was screened overseas or had a negative screen: **still do a sweat test**.
- **Nasal polyps in a child** are CF until proven otherwise.
- Meconium ileus in a newborn: think CF.
- Hyponatraemic hypochloraemic alkalosis in a CF infant in summer: salt depletion; salt supplements.
- Risk calculations: 1 in 4 affected; unaffected sibling 2 in 3 carrier.
- CFTR modulators are PBS-subsidised for eligible patients.

keyPoints: Autosomal recessive CFTR mutation on chromosome 7; F508del commonest; about 1 in 25 carriers of European ancestry.
Newborn screening: IRT then DNA testing; a positive screen needs a sweat test.
Sweat chloride 60 mmol/L or more confirms CF; 30-59 intermediate.
Symptoms of CF need a sweat test even if the newborn screen was negative.
Management: airway clearance, antibiotics, enzymes with meals, high-fat diet, ADEK vitamins, salt.
CFTR modulators (elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor) are PBS-subsidised for eligible patients.
Carrier screening for CF, SMA and fragile X is offered before or early in pregnancy.
redFlags: Meconium ileus in a newborn
Failure to thrive with steatorrhoea
Nasal polyps in a child
Chronic wet cough or recurrent pneumonia
Hyponatraemic dehydration in hot weather

contrast.india: Often diagnosed late, after years of failure to thrive or chest infections; sweat testing limited.
contrast.australia: Diagnosed through universal newborn screening, confirmed with a sweat chloride test at a CF centre.
Carrier screening for CF, SMA and fragile X offered to all planning or early in pregnancy, with Medicare rebate.

flashcards.front: Screening test for CF in newborn bloodspot?
flashcards.back: Immunoreactive trypsinogen (IRT), then CFTR mutation testing.

flashcards.front: Sweat chloride level diagnostic of CF?
flashcards.back: 60 mmol/L or more.

flashcards.front: Chance an unaffected sibling of a child with CF is a carrier?
flashcards.back: 2 in 3.

flashcards.front: Electrolyte disturbance in CF with heat exposure?
flashcards.back: Hyponatraemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis (salt loss in sweat).

flashcards.front: Cause of infertility in males with CF?
flashcards.back: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens.

quiz.stem: A 3-week-old boy is referred because his newborn bloodspot screen showed a raised immunoreactive trypsinogen and one CFTR mutation (F508del) detected. He is feeding well and gaining weight. What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Chest X-ray
Faecal elastase only
Sweat chloride test
Repeat heel prick at 6 months
Serum immunoglobulins
quiz.explanation:
A positive newborn screen is **not a diagnosis**. With a raised IRT and one mutation, the baby may have CF (with a second mutation not on the panel) or be a healthy **carrier**. The confirmatory test is the **sweat chloride test** at a CF centre: **60 mmol/L or more** is consistent with CF, 30-59 intermediate, under 30 unlikely.

If he is a carrier, his parents are offered testing and genetic counselling. Faecal elastase assesses pancreatic function once CF is confirmed.
whyWrong: A chest X-ray does not diagnose CF.
Faecal elastase tests pancreatic function, not the diagnosis.
Delaying diagnosis is inappropriate; a sweat test is needed now.
Immunoglobulins are for immunodeficiency, not CF.

quiz.stem: A 4-year-old boy who arrived from overseas a year ago has had recurrent chest infections and a persistent wet cough. He has a big appetite but is below the 3rd centile for weight, and his stools are pale, bulky and difficult to flush. On examination he has nasal polyps and mild finger clubbing. His parents are unsure whether he was screened as a newborn. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Sweat chloride test
Coeliac serology only and gluten-free diet
Trial of inhaled corticosteroids
Reassure and review growth in 6 months
Chest CT scan
quiz.explanation:
Failure to thrive with **steatorrhoea** despite a good appetite, **chronic wet cough**, recurrent chest infections, **nasal polyps** and **clubbing** in a child point strongly to **cystic fibrosis**. Nasal polyps in a child are CF until proven otherwise.

Because newborn screening is not universal worldwide (and misses rare mutations even in Australia), any child with suggestive symptoms needs a **sweat chloride test**, regardless of screening history. Then refer to a CF centre for management including enzymes, nutrition and airway clearance.
whyWrong: Coeliac disease doesn't cause nasal polyps or chronic wet cough; don't start a diet before testing.
This is not asthma; wet cough, clubbing and steatorrhoea suggest CF.
He has faltering growth and chronic lung disease; delay is harmful.
CT may show bronchiectasis later but doesn't make the diagnosis.

quiz.stem: A couple's first child has cystic fibrosis. Neither parent has CF. Their 8-year-old daughter is healthy and has a normal sweat test. The daughter's future partner is from the general population of European ancestry, with an estimated carrier frequency of 1 in 25. What is the approximate risk that the daughter's first child will have CF, assuming no testing?
options: 1 in 4
1 in 50
quiz.explanation:
Both parents are obligate carriers. An **unaffected** child of two carriers has a **2 in 3** chance of being a carrier (the affected outcome is excluded by her normal sweat test, leaving carrier, carrier, non-carrier).

Risk for her child = (her carrier probability 2/3) x (partner carrier probability 1/25) x (chance two carriers have an affected child 1/4) = 2/300 = **1 in 150**.

This is why **carrier testing** is offered to relatives of people with CF, and why reproductive carrier screening (CF, SMA, fragile X) is offered to couples planning pregnancy in Australia. If both are carriers, options include prenatal diagnosis or preimplantation genetic testing.
whyWrong: 1 in 4 applies only when both partners are known carriers.
This ignores the 1 in 4 risk when both are carriers.
This assumes she is definitely a carrier (1 x 1/25 x 1/4).
This is roughly the general population birth prevalence, ignoring her family history.

lessons.title: ADHD and neurodevelopmental concerns
objectives: Apply DSM-5 criteria for ADHD, including onset before 12 and symptoms in more than one setting
Assess a child with suspected ADHD and exclude common mimics and comorbidities
Outline non-drug and drug management, including stimulant monitoring and state regulation
Distinguish ADHD from autism, learning disorders, anxiety and trauma

sections.heading: ADHD in Australia
sections.body:
**Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)** is the most common neurodevelopmental disorder of childhood, affecting around **6-8% of Australian children and adolescents**, more commonly diagnosed in boys (girls are underdiagnosed, often presenting with inattention rather than hyperactivity). It is highly heritable and persists into adulthood in many.

The **Australian Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guideline for ADHD** (AADPA, 2022) guides care. Stimulant medicines are **Schedule 8** (controlled drugs), and **prescribing rules are set by each state and territory**: traditionally, a paediatrician or psychiatrist diagnoses and initiates, and GPs may continue prescribing under shared-care arrangements or permits. Several states have recently expanded the role of GPs, so **the rules vary by state**.

sections.heading: Diagnosis (DSM-5)
sections.body:
**Two symptom domains**:
- **Inattention**: careless mistakes, can't sustain attention, doesn't seem to listen, doesn't finish tasks, disorganised, avoids sustained mental effort, loses things, easily distracted, forgetful.
- **Hyperactivity-impulsivity**: fidgets, leaves seat, runs or climbs inappropriately, can't play quietly, "on the go", talks excessively, blurts out answers, can't wait turn, interrupts.

**Criteria**:
- **At least 6 symptoms** in one or both domains (**5 for age 17 and over**), for **at least 6 months**, inappropriate for developmental level.
- **Several symptoms present before age 12.**
- Symptoms present in **two or more settings** (home, school, with friends).
- Clear **impairment** in social, academic or occupational functioning.
- Not better explained by another condition.

Presentations: **combined**, **predominantly inattentive**, or **predominantly hyperactive-impulsive**.

**Assessment**:
- History from parents, **school reports and teacher input** (structured rating scales such as Conners or Vanderbilt questionnaires from parent and teacher).
- Developmental, family (ADHD often runs in families), social and psychosocial history (trauma, family stress).
- Examination: growth, dysmorphism, neurocutaneous signs, **hearing and vision**, BP and heart rate (baseline for medication).
- Look for **mimics and comorbidities** (next section).

sections.heading: Mimics and comorbidities
sections.body:
More than half of children with ADHD have at least one comorbidity, and several conditions mimic it.

| Condition | Clues |
|---|---|
| **Autism spectrum disorder** | Persistent deficits in **social communication** and **restricted, repetitive behaviours or interests** (insistence on sameness, sensory sensitivities). Can co-exist with ADHD |
| **Specific learning disorder** (dyslexia, dyscalculia) | Inattention mainly during literacy or maths tasks; psychoeducational testing |
| **Intellectual disability** | Global delay; attention consistent with developmental age |
| **Anxiety or depression** | Worry, avoidance, poor concentration from internal preoccupation |
| **Trauma, neglect, family violence** | Hypervigilance, dysregulation; ask sensitively |
| **Obstructive sleep apnoea / poor sleep** | Snoring, restless sleep, daytime tiredness; hyperactivity is a common daytime feature in children |
| **Hearing or vision impairment** | Doesn't follow instructions |
| **Absence epilepsy** | Brief staring episodes, many times a day |
| **Oppositional defiant or conduct disorder** | Defiance and rule-breaking (frequently comorbid) |
| Tic disorders, thyroid disease, medications, substance use in adolescents | |
| **Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder** | Prenatal alcohol exposure; important in some communities; growth and facial features may or may not be present |

**Autism** in brief: diagnosis is by a paediatrician, psychiatrist or multidisciplinary team, using DSM-5 criteria; early intervention is key. Australia's **National Guideline for the Assessment and Diagnosis of Autism** guides the process, and many children access support through the **NDIS** (National Disability Insurance Scheme). Red flags in toddlers: no babbling or pointing by 12 months, no single words by 16-18 months, no two-word phrases by 24 months, and **any loss of language or social skills at any age**.

sections.heading: Management
sections.body:
**Non-pharmacological (always)**
- **Psychoeducation** for the child and family.
- **Parent training programs** (for example Triple P, developed in Australia), particularly for preschoolers, where they are first-line.
- **School supports**: classroom strategies, seating near the teacher, breaking tasks down, individual learning plans; teachers are key partners.
- Treat comorbidities; sleep hygiene; exercise; social skills support.

**Medication** is recommended for school-aged children and adolescents with ADHD causing significant impairment, alongside non-drug measures. Medication in preschoolers is a specialist decision after behavioural approaches.

| Class | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Stimulants (first line)** | **Methylphenidate**, **dexamfetamine**, **lisdexamfetamine** | Schedule 8; state permits/authority; PBS criteria |
| Non-stimulants | **Atomoxetine**, **guanfacine** (extended release), clonidine | Useful with tics, anxiety, substance misuse concerns, or stimulant intolerance |

**Before starting stimulants**: baseline **height, weight, BP and heart rate**; ask about **cardiac history** (syncope with exercise, palpitations, chest pain, known heart disease, **family history of sudden cardiac death** or inherited arrhythmias). ECG and cardiology referral if any of these are present.

**Side effects**: **reduced appetite** and weight loss (give medication with or after breakfast, encourage a big evening meal), **insomnia**, headache, abdominal pain, irritability or "rebound" in the evening, raised heart rate and BP, and possible slowing of growth. Tics may be unmasked. Rarely psychosis or mood changes.

**Monitoring**: height, weight (on centile charts), BP and heart rate at least every 6 months; review benefit and side effects with parent and teacher reports; consider planned breaks where appropriate. Watch for **diversion** of stimulants in adolescents (they are drugs of misuse).

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Hyperactive only at school, fine at home and with friends: **does not meet the two-setting criterion**; think learning disorder, classroom factors or other causes.
- Symptoms starting at 15 with no childhood history: doesn't meet "several symptoms before age 12"; look for depression, substance use, sleep problems.
- Snoring child with inattention and hyperactivity: consider **OSA** (adenotonsillar hypertrophy) before ADHD medication.
- Before a stimulant: **ask about family history of sudden cardiac death and exercise syncope**; measure BP, HR, height and weight.
- Commonest stimulant side effect: **appetite suppression** (and insomnia).
- Stimulants are **Schedule 8**; prescribing rules **vary by state**.
- Preschooler with hyperactivity: **parent training first**.

keyPoints: ADHD affects about 6-8% of Australian children; girls are often inattentive and underdiagnosed.
DSM-5: 6 or more symptoms (5 from age 17) for 6 months, several before age 12, in two or more settings, with impairment.
Always gather teacher information and check hearing, vision, sleep and comorbidities.
Common mimics: learning disorders, OSA, anxiety, trauma, absence epilepsy, autism.
Parent training first in preschoolers; medication plus behavioural support in school-aged children.
Stimulants are Schedule 8; initiation rules and permits vary by state.
Monitor height, weight, BP and heart rate; ask about cardiac history and family sudden death before starting.
redFlags: Loss of previously acquired language or social skills
Exercise-related syncope or family history of sudden cardiac death before stimulants
Suspected abuse, neglect or family violence behind behavioural change
Stimulant diversion or misuse in an adolescent

contrast.india: Psychiatrists prescribe methylphenidate; access and cost vary widely.
contrast.australia: Schedule 8 with state-based permits; paediatrician or psychiatrist initiation traditionally, GP roles expanding in some states.

contrast.india: Limited early intervention services outside cities.
contrast.australia: Formal diagnostic guideline and NDIS funding for early intervention and therapy supports.

flashcards.back: Two or more (for example home and school).

flashcards.back: Stimulants: methylphenidate, dexamfetamine or lisdexamfetamine.

flashcards.front: Most common side effects of stimulants?
flashcards.back: Reduced appetite (weight loss) and insomnia.

flashcards.front: What must be asked before starting a stimulant?
flashcards.back: Cardiac history: exercise syncope, palpitations, heart disease, family history of sudden cardiac death.

flashcards.front: First-line treatment for ADHD symptoms in a preschooler?
flashcards.back: Parent training programs (for example Triple P).

quiz.stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought in because his teacher says he cannot sit still, interrupts constantly and doesn't finish work. His parents say he is 'the same at home since kindergarten': losing things, not listening, climbing on furniture, and struggling at soccer practice. Hearing and vision are normal and there is no snoring. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start methylphenidate today
Tell the parents he will grow out of it
Refer for comprehensive assessment by a paediatrician, with parent and teacher rating scales
Arrange an EEG
Arrange thyroid function tests and review
quiz.explanation:
He has symptoms of inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity **since before age 12**, in **more than one setting** (school, home, sport), with **impairment**. This fits ADHD, but the diagnosis needs a **comprehensive assessment**: structured parent and teacher rating scales (for example Conners or Vanderbilt), developmental and family history, and screening for comorbidities and mimics (learning disorder, anxiety, autism, trauma).

In Australia, the diagnosis and initiation of stimulants is usually by a **paediatrician or psychiatrist**, with GP involvement varying by state. Starting medication without assessment is inappropriate, and routine EEG or thyroid tests are not indicated without specific features.
whyWrong: Stimulants should not be started before a proper assessment, and state rules usually require specialist initiation.
ADHD often persists; dismissal delays help.
EEG is only needed if absences or seizures are suspected.
Thyroid disease is a rare cause and routine testing isn't needed without other features.

quiz.stem: A 7-year-old girl is referred by her school because of inattention, fidgeting and daytime tiredness. Her mother reports that she snores loudly most nights, with pauses in breathing, and wets the bed occasionally. She breathes through her mouth and has large tonsils on examination. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Start a stimulant medication trial
Start melatonin
Refer to a psychologist for behavioural therapy only
Refer for assessment of obstructive sleep apnoea (ENT and/or sleep study)
Start atomoxetine
quiz.explanation:
**Obstructive sleep apnoea** from **adenotonsillar hypertrophy** is a common, treatable mimic of ADHD in children. Unlike adults, children with OSA often show **hyperactivity, inattention and behavioural problems** rather than obvious sleepiness. Loud nightly snoring with witnessed pauses, mouth breathing, enuresis and large tonsils strongly suggest it.

She should be referred to **ENT** (and/or for a **sleep study**); adenotonsillectomy often improves both sleep and daytime behaviour. ADHD can then be reassessed if symptoms persist.
whyWrong: Stimulants don't treat OSA and could worsen sleep.
Melatonin doesn't treat airway obstruction.
Behavioural therapy alone misses a treatable medical cause.
ADHD medication is premature before excluding OSA.

quiz.stem: A 10-year-old boy with newly diagnosed ADHD is about to start methylphenidate. His father mentions that the boy fainted twice during swimming carnivals last year, and that the boy's uncle died suddenly aged 24 while jogging. His examination, BP and heart rate are normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange an ECG and cardiology review before starting stimulant medication
Start atomoxetine instead, without further testing
Start methylphenidate at a low dose and review in 4 weeks
Reassure; fainting is common in children
Arrange an EEG for the fainting episodes
quiz.explanation:
Stimulants increase heart rate and BP, so before starting them clinicians ask about **cardiac red flags**: **exertional syncope**, palpitations, chest pain, known heart disease, and **family history of sudden cardiac death at a young age**. This boy has both **syncope during exercise (swimming)** and a **young relative's sudden death during exertion**, raising concern for an inherited arrhythmia or cardiomyopathy (for example **long QT syndrome**, where swimming is a classic trigger, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy).

He needs an **ECG and cardiology assessment** before any ADHD medication, whether stimulant or non-stimulant. The finding also matters for his own safety irrespective of ADHD.
whyWrong: Atomoxetine also affects heart rate and BP; cardiac assessment is still needed.
Starting a stimulant with unexplained exertional syncope and a family history of sudden death is unsafe.
Exertional syncope is a cardiac red flag, not benign fainting.
The concern is cardiac, not epileptic.

lessons.title: Acute rheumatic fever and rheumatic heart disease
objectives: Explain how group A streptococcal infection leads to ARF and RHD, and why it clusters in remote Australia
Diagnose ARF using the Australian Jones criteria for high-risk and low-risk groups
Manage an acute episode and prescribe long-term benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis
Describe primary prevention, RHD registers and community approaches

sections.heading: An Australian health equity issue
sections.body:
Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) has almost disappeared from wealthy populations, but **Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people**, especially children and young adults in **remote northern and central Australia** (NT, far north Queensland, the Kimberley and Pilbara in WA, and SA), have **some of the highest rates of ARF and rheumatic heart disease (RHD) in the world**. Māori and Pacific Islander communities, and migrants from high-prevalence countries (including parts of South Asia), are also at higher risk.

The driving factors are social: **household crowding, inadequate housing and hygiene facilities**, and poverty, which increase group A streptococcal (GAS) transmission, including through **skin sores (impetigo) and scabies**. RHD causes heart failure, stroke, endocarditis and pregnancy complications, and premature death.

Australian care follows the **RHDAustralia guideline** (The 2020 Australian guideline for prevention, diagnosis and management of ARF and RHD, 3rd edition). **ARF and RHD are notifiable** in several states and territories, and **state RHD registers** coordinate prophylaxis and follow-up (details vary by jurisdiction).

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.body:
ARF is an **autoimmune** reaction 2-4 weeks after GAS infection. Antibodies and T cells against streptococcal antigens (especially the **M protein**) cross-react with host tissues (**molecular mimicry**): cardiac myosin and valve tissue, synovium, basal ganglia neurons (Sydenham chorea) and skin.

- Classically after **GAS pharyngitis**; in remote Australian communities, **GAS skin infection** is also thought to contribute.
- **Carditis** affects all layers (pancarditis), but the lasting damage is to the **valves**: the **mitral valve** most often (mitral regurgitation acutely; mitral stenosis after years), then the aortic valve.
- Each **recurrence** of ARF causes further valve damage, which is why **secondary prophylaxis** is the most important intervention after diagnosis.
- Arthritis and chorea resolve without permanent damage; the heart is what matters long term.

sections.heading: Diagnosis: the Australian Jones criteria
sections.body:
Australia uses **different thresholds for high-risk and low-risk groups** (making it more sensitive where ARF is common):

- **High-risk**: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in rural or remote settings, Māori and Pacific Islander people, and others living in high-risk settings (for example crowding, or migrants from high-prevalence countries).
- **Low-risk**: everyone else.

| | High-risk groups | Low-risk groups |
|---|---|---|
| **Major** | **Carditis** (including subclinical, found on echo); **polyarthritis, aseptic monoarthritis or polyarthralgia**; **Sydenham chorea**; erythema marginatum; subcutaneous nodules | Carditis (including subclinical); **polyarthritis** only; chorea; erythema marginatum; subcutaneous nodules |
| **Minor** | **Monoarthralgia**; fever **38.0 °C or more**; ESR 30 mm/h or more, or CRP 30 mg/L or more; prolonged PR interval | **Polyarthralgia or aseptic monoarthritis**; fever **38.5 °C or more**; ESR 60 mm/h or more, or CRP 30 mg/L or more; prolonged PR interval |

**Diagnosis of a first episode**: evidence of **preceding GAS infection** (raised or rising **ASOT or anti-DNase B**, or positive culture/PCR) plus **2 major**, or **1 major and 2 minor** criteria. **Sydenham chorea** can be diagnosed alone without other criteria or evidence of GAS, because it can appear months after the infection.

(Check the RHDAustralia guideline for the exact current criteria and for recurrent ARF, where the thresholds are lower.)

**Clinical pictures the AMC uses**:
- A 10-year-old Aboriginal child from a remote community with **fever and a migratory painful swollen joint** (large joints, moving from knee to ankle to elbow over days), responding dramatically to NSAIDs.
- **Carditis**: new murmur (apical pansystolic of mitral regurgitation), tachycardia out of proportion to fever, pericardial rub, heart failure.
- **Sydenham chorea**: purposeless jerky movements, emotional lability, "milkmaid's grip", deteriorating handwriting, typically in girls; may appear alone months after infection.
- **Erythema marginatum**: pink rings with clear centres on the trunk (hard to see on dark skin); **subcutaneous nodules** over extensor surfaces.

**Investigations**: ASOT and anti-DNase B (repeat after 10-14 days for rising titre), throat swab, **ESR and CRP**, FBC, **ECG** (prolonged PR), **echocardiogram** in every suspected case (subclinical carditis counts as a major criterion), and blood cultures if febrile (to exclude endocarditis). Differentials include septic arthritis, reactive arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, viral arthritis, and leukaemia (bone pain).

sections.heading: Treatment and prophylaxis
sections.body:
**Acute episode** (admit to hospital, ideally where echo is available):
- **Eradicate GAS**: benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM (single dose), which also counts as the first prophylactic dose; oral penicillin if IM is refused.
- **Arthritis/fever**: NSAIDs (**naproxen** is commonly used in current Australian guidance; aspirin is an alternative). Joint pain responds dramatically; lack of response should prompt a rethink. Holding NSAIDs until the diagnosis is clear can help the joint pattern declare itself, with paracetamol meanwhile.
- **Carditis/heart failure**: diuretics, ACE inhibitors, specialist care; corticosteroids may be considered for severe carditis; valve surgery if needed.
- **Chorea**: usually self-limited over weeks to months; medication (for example carbamazepine or valproate) for severe cases.
- Register with the state **RHD register** and notify where required.
- Education for the family, and a plan for dental review.

**Secondary prophylaxis (the key intervention)**:
- **Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days** (every 21 days for some high-risk patients).
- Duration (RHDAustralia): at least **10 years after the last ARF episode or until age 21, whichever is longer**, for ARF without cardiac involvement or with mild RHD; **longer (to age 35 or 40, or longer)** for moderate or severe RHD. Check the guideline for the exact table.
- Penicillin allergy: specialist allergy assessment is recommended, as true allergy is uncommon; erythromycin is an oral alternative.
- Reducing injection pain (lignocaine mixed with the penicillin where allowed, ice, distraction, warming to room temperature) improves adherence.
- **Adherence** is the major challenge; Aboriginal health workers and practitioners, community-controlled services and registers with recall systems are essential.

**Other ongoing care**: regular echocardiography and specialist review, **dental care** (oral health reduces endocarditis risk), **endocarditis prophylaxis** for dental procedures in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with RHD (eTG), influenza vaccination, pregnancy planning and contraception (RHD in pregnancy is high risk), and anticoagulation for AF or mechanical valves.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.body:
- **Primordial**: better housing, less crowding, functional washing facilities, healthy skin programs (treating scabies and impetigo).
- **Primary**: treat **GAS sore throat and skin sores** promptly in high-risk populations with penicillin (benzathine benzylpenicillin IM once, or oral phenoxymethylpenicillin for 10 days). In high-risk settings, a sore throat in a child is treated as possible GAS.
- **Secondary**: long-term benzathine benzylpenicillin for anyone with ARF or RHD.
- **Tertiary**: echo surveillance, heart failure care, valve surgery.
- **Echocardiographic screening** in high-risk communities has been used in research and programs to find subclinical RHD.

sections.heading: How the AMC asks this
sections.body:
- Aboriginal child from a remote community with fever and a **single swollen joint or polyarthralgia**: in high-risk groups these count as **major** criteria. Do an echo.
- Every suspected ARF case needs an **echocardiogram** (subclinical carditis is a major criterion).
- **Chorea alone** is enough to diagnose ARF.
- Most important long-term treatment: **benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days** for at least 10 years or until 21 (longer with moderate/severe RHD).
- Mitral regurgitation is the commonest valve lesion.
- A dramatic response to NSAIDs supports ARF arthritis; no response suggests another diagnosis.
- RHD registers and notification: know that they exist and vary by state.

keyPoints: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in remote northern and central Australia have among the highest ARF/RHD rates in the world.
ARF is autoimmune (molecular mimicry) 2-4 weeks after GAS throat or possibly skin infection.
Australian Jones criteria use lower thresholds for high-risk groups (monoarthritis or polyarthralgia can be major).
Diagnosis: evidence of GAS plus 2 major, or 1 major and 2 minor; chorea alone suffices.
Echocardiogram for every suspected case; subclinical carditis counts.
Secondary prophylaxis: benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days, at least 10 years or to age 21, longer for moderate or severe RHD.
Mitral valve is most often affected; dental care and endocarditis prophylaxis matter.
redFlags: New murmur or heart failure in a child with arthritis and fever
Fever with joint pain in a high-risk child (don't dismiss as a sprain)
Chorea or new emotional lability in a school-aged child
Missed benzathine penicillin doses in a patient with RHD
Pregnancy in a woman with RHD

contrast.india: ARF and RHD remain common, especially in poorer rural populations.
contrast.australia: Rare in most Australians but very high in remote Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities; notifiable and registered in several states.

contrast.india: Revised Jones criteria (AHA 2015) with WHO guidance.
contrast.australia: Australian guideline criteria with separate high-risk and low-risk thresholds (RHDAustralia 2020).

contrast.india: Benzathine penicillin often limited by supply and fear of reactions.
contrast.australia: 4-weekly benzathine benzylpenicillin G supported by registers, recall systems and Aboriginal health workers.

flashcards.front: Most important long-term treatment after ARF?
flashcards.back: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days (secondary prophylaxis).

flashcards.front: Minimum duration of prophylaxis after ARF with no or mild carditis (RHDAustralia)?
flashcards.back: 10 years after the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer.

flashcards.front: Which ARF feature can establish the diagnosis on its own?
flashcards.back: Sydenham chorea.

flashcards.front: Which joint presentations count as major criteria in high-risk groups?
flashcards.back: Polyarthritis, aseptic monoarthritis or polyarthralgia.

flashcards.front: Commonest valve affected in RHD?
flashcards.back: Mitral valve (regurgitation early, stenosis later).

flashcards.front: Investigation needed in every suspected ARF case?
flashcards.back: Echocardiogram (subclinical carditis counts as a major criterion).

quiz.stem: A 9-year-old Aboriginal boy from a remote community in the Northern Territory presents with 4 days of fever (38.4 °C) and a painful, swollen right knee. He had skin sores on his legs a month ago. ASOT is markedly raised, CRP is 85 mg/L and the ECG shows a prolonged PR interval. Joint aspirate is sterile. Echocardiography is pending. Under the Australian criteria, what is the best interpretation?
options: ARF cannot be diagnosed without polyarthritis
Definite ARF: one major criterion (aseptic monoarthritis) and two or more minor criteria, with evidence of GAS infection
Septic arthritis; start IV flucloxacillin and no further workup
Reactive arthritis; NSAIDs only, no penicillin
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis; refer to rheumatology
quiz.explanation:
In **high-risk groups** (Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in remote settings), the Australian criteria count **aseptic monoarthritis** as a **major** criterion. His **minor** criteria include fever of 38.0 °C or more, **CRP of 30 mg/L or more**, and a **prolonged PR interval**. With evidence of **preceding GAS infection** (raised ASOT), **1 major plus 2 minor** criteria meet the definition of ARF.

The lower thresholds exist because ARF is common in these communities and missing it means missing secondary prophylaxis. He needs an **echocardiogram** (subclinical carditis would add a second major criterion), GAS eradication with benzathine benzylpenicillin, NSAIDs, registration and long-term prophylaxis.
whyWrong: In high-risk groups monoarthritis counts as a major criterion.
The aspirate is sterile; ARF is the likely diagnosis in this setting.
Reactive arthritis doesn't explain raised ASOT with prolonged PR in this context, and missing ARF withholds prophylaxis.
JIA requires arthritis for at least 6 weeks and doesn't fit the acute post-streptococcal picture.
quiz.ausPearl: Australian ARF criteria use lower thresholds in high-risk populations (RHDAustralia 2020 guideline).

quiz.stem: A 14-year-old Torres Strait Islander girl was diagnosed with acute rheumatic fever with mild mitral regurgitation 6 months ago. She is well. Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
options: Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days for at least 10 years after the last episode or until age 21, whichever is longer
Oral amoxicillin only when she has a sore throat
Benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days for 12 months only
Daily aspirin for life
No treatment unless symptoms recur
quiz.explanation:
The most important intervention after ARF is **secondary prophylaxis** to prevent recurrences, each of which causes further valve damage. The first-line regimen is **benzathine benzylpenicillin G IM every 28 days** (21 days for some high-risk patients).

For ARF with no or **mild** carditis, the RHDAustralia guideline recommends at least **10 years after the most recent episode or until age 21, whichever is longer**. With moderate or severe RHD, prophylaxis continues longer (to 35 or 40 years of age or beyond). She also needs regular echocardiography, dental care, endocarditis prophylaxis for dental procedures, registration on the RHD register, and pregnancy planning advice.
whyWrong: Treating sore throats alone doesn't prevent recurrences reliably.
12 months is far too short.
Aspirin treats arthritis acutely; it doesn't prevent recurrence.
Without prophylaxis, recurrences and progressive valve damage are likely.

quiz.stem: An 11-year-old girl who moved from a Pacific Island nation 2 years ago has had 3 weeks of clumsiness, dropping things and writing that has become messy. Her mother reports she has become tearful and irritable. On examination there are irregular, purposeless jerky movements of her face and hands, and her grip waxes and wanes when squeezing the examiner's fingers. She is afebrile. ASOT is normal. What is the most appropriate management?
options: Reassure; ARF can't be diagnosed with a normal ASOT
Diagnose Sydenham chorea (ARF), arrange echocardiography and start benzathine benzylpenicillin prophylaxis
Start haloperidol and discharge
Refer for psychological therapy for a functional disorder
Arrange genetic testing for Huntington disease
quiz.explanation:
Purposeless jerky movements, **"milkmaid's grip"**, deteriorating handwriting and **emotional lability** are classic **Sydenham chorea**. Chorea can appear **months after** the GAS infection, when streptococcal antibodies may have normalised, so **chorea alone is sufficient to diagnose ARF** without other criteria or serological evidence.

She needs an **echocardiogram** (carditis often coexists, sometimes subclinically), **benzathine benzylpenicillin** (eradication and then 4-weekly secondary prophylaxis), and symptomatic treatment if chorea is severe (for example carbamazepine or valproate). She is from a high-risk group (Pacific Islander).
whyWrong: Chorea can occur after antibody levels normalise; it diagnoses ARF on its own.
Symptomatic treatment alone misses the need for echo and prophylaxis.
This is a recognisable organic movement disorder.
Huntington disease in childhood is very rare and wouldn't explain this subacute picture in a high-risk child.
